clue.text: Very legitimate request

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, 'a very legitimate request', but it splits into two adjectives stacked in front of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to ask for something, often formally or persistently.

clue.text: School team met regularly for project

parts.note: SCH is the standard abbreviation for school

indicators.note: 'regularly' asks for letters at even intervals, here every second letter of 'team met'

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of tEaMmEt

explanation.surface: A school side gathers routinely to work on some joint undertaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team met' is not a noun and verb here; it is just a string of letters to be thinned out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name a planned undertaking, as in a housing scheme.

clue.text: Needing no introduction, cholera devastated Asian city

indicators.note: devastated means wrecked, so the remaining letters are rearranged
needing no introduction says the word loses its opening letter

explanation.surface: A disease outbreak that needs no explaining has ravaged a city in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing no introduction' leaves HOLERA, which 'devastated' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Lahore is a major city in Pakistan, capital of Punjab province.

clue.text: Contrast second century uprising with Trojan one, briefly

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for century

indicators.note: in a down clue, something rising reads from the bottom up

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a second; it goes upward to give OM
Paris, the Trojan prince who carried off Helen

indicators.note: 'briefly' cuts a letter off

explanation.surface: A historian compares a second-century revolt with the Trojan War.
explanation.walkthrough: The century does not follow 'second' as the surface implies: 'second' gives MO and 'century' gives C, and the reversed MO comes after C.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparison is a contrast drawn between two things.

clue.text: Unexpected event in second part of Dickens novel

definitions.meaning: the surprise turn a plot takes near the end
the second word of the title of Dickens's novel about the workhouse orphan Oliver

explanation.walkthrough: The novel is Oliver Twist, so its second word is TWIST; the surface hints at a plot turn inside the book.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sense is the plot-turn idiom; the second is the orphan's surname in the book's title.

clue.text: Meat starter in vegetarian function returned — concerning!

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter
a word returned goes back the way it came

parts.note: sine is a trigonometric function; returned it gives ENIS

explanation.surface: A meat starter served at a vegetarian event is sent back, a worrying mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Function' looks like a dinner event, but it is the mathematical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: deer meat is one kind of meat, a game meat the vegetarian in the surface would certainly send back.

clue.text: Crime-fighter mutilated evil giant

indicators.note: something mutilated is torn apart, its letters left out of order

explanation.surface: A comic-book hero maims a wicked giant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mutilated' fits the violent surface, but here it only scrambles the letters of 'evil giant'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vigilante fights crime without legal authority.

clue.text: Reportedly, German's negative figure

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so we go by sound

explanation.surface: A German is said to have produced a gloomy number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Negative figure' looks like a minus number, but the negative belongs to the German.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: 'figure' means a numeral, and this is one of the digits.

clue.text: Occasional police operations set up with armed soldiers involved

indicators.note: the soldiers are involved in, taken inside, the other letters
in a down clue, set up means written bottom to top

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the UK detective branch
RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners

explanation.surface: Police raids happen now and then, with armed troops brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police operations' reads as one idea, raids, and a solver may try to fit RAIDS; the pair splits into two abbreviations instead. CID is the British detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporadic means occasional, happening at irregular intervals.

clue.text: Moving gingerly to pinch the Queen's jewellery

explanation.surface: A thief creeps forward carefully to steal the royal jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinch' suggests stealing, which suits the Crown Jewels in the surface, but here it only means to hold tight.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a ring worn through a pierced nostril is one kind of jewellery.

clue.text: Routine Groucho humorously displays

indicators.note: the phrase displays, puts on show, letters already inside it

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the comedian's name into the start of the adverb

explanation.surface: Groucho Marx shows off a comic routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Routine' looks like a comedian's act, which fits Groucho, but it means dull and ordinary.
explanation.definitionFit: Ho-hum describes something routine and boring.

clue.text: Brilliant new information welcomed by one with debts

indicators.note: welcomed by says these letters are taken in by the letters for one with debts

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
IOUs are written notes of debt
gen is informal British slang for information

explanation.surface: Some clever fresh news is warmly received by a debtor.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingenious idea is clever and inventive, which is a sense of brilliant.

clue.text: Dealing with trade in lace, term that's unusual

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement is not the normal order of the letters

explanation.surface: A lace trader uses an odd piece of jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trade in lace' looks like a phrase about the lace business, but the definition ends at 'trade'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercantile means relating to trade and merchants.

clue.text: Couple accompanying piano with song

indicators.note: one thing accompanying another goes alongside it

parts.note: an air is a tune or song

explanation.surface: A duo performs a song with piano backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accompanying' looks like a musical term here, but it just says P goes with AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns mean two things or people taken together.

clue.text: Except individual, content to assess peers

parts.note: bar = except, as in 'all bar one'

indicators.note: the content of a word is what lies inside it, its middle letters

explanation.surface: Everyone except one person is happy to judge their equals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as 'happy to', but it means the contents of 'assess'. 'Peers' looks like equals; it is members of the House of Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Baronesses are female peers, members of the British peerage.

clue.text: After I'd retired, quietly admitted to feeling relief

indicators.note: retiring is withdrawing backward, so ID goes back to DI

parts.note: I'd written as ID; retired it gives DI

explanation.surface: Once retired, someone quietly confessed to a sense of relief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted to feeling' reads as confessing an emotion; it means P is let into SENSATION.
explanation.definitionFit: A dispensation is a relief or exemption from a rule or obligation.

clue.text: Sponsorship a pro agent sorted out

indicators.note: sorting things out rearranges them

explanation.surface: A sports professional's agent arranges a sponsorship deal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is so plausible that the fodder, 'a pro agent', reads as a real person rather than nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean the financial backing a patron or sponsor gives.

clue.text: Becomes emotional entering hotel to drink with another

indicators.note: the hotel enters, goes inside, the drink

parts.note: H is Hotel in the phonetic alphabet
to sup is to drink, a second drink word

explanation.surface: Someone gets tearful walking into a hotel to have a drink with a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With another' reads as drinking with a friend, but 'another' is a second drink word, and the enumeration (6,2) marks where it joins.
explanation.definitionFit: To choke up is to become too emotional to speak.

clue.text: Vital safeguard with large cat south of island

indicators.note: in a down entry, south is lower down the grid, so the cat is written below the island

parts.note: L = large, as on clothing sizes

explanation.surface: A big cat on an island is protected as a vital measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large cat' wants to be a lion or tiger; 'large' is L on its own. In a down clue, 'south of' puts FELINE below I.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeline is something vital that keeps you safe.

clue.text: Hangover cure that's taken from best friend's coat

definitions.meaning: a morning drink to ease a hangover
the dog is man's best friend, and its coat is hair

explanation.walkthrough: The dog is man's best friend, and its coat is its hair. The link 'that's taken from' plays on the phrase's origin: a hair from the dog that bit you.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a morning drink against a hangover, from the old remedy of a hair from the dog that bit you; literally, a dog's coat.

clue.text: Blot last bit of text in Greek letter

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A scribe blots the end of a manuscript in Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blot' looks like a verb for smudging ink, but it is a noun: a stain on a reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: A stigma is a blot or stain on one's reputation.

clue.text: Cave with base becoming variable and rough

indicators.note: becoming says the base letter turns into the variable

parts.note: in a down clue the base of the word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A cave whose floor has become shifting and uneven.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the 'base' is the bottom letter, the final O of GROTTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotty is British slang for unpleasant or shabby, a sense close to rough.

clue.text: Understood novel to be in audio version

indicators.note: an audio version is heard, so we go by sound

explanation.surface: Someone grasped that a novel would be released as an audiobook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, which suits the audio version, but it means new.
explanation.definitionFit: Knew is the past tense of know, so it means understood.

clue.text: Nothing against landlord's romantic reading material

indicators.note: one thing set against another is placed right beside it

parts.note: a letter is someone who lets property, a landlord

explanation.surface: A landlord's taste in romance novels comes under criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: Love means zero in tennis scoring. The landlord here is literally one who lets property, a sense only crosswords use.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a note between sweethearts is one kind of romantic thing to read.

clue.text: Standing straight before court

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A defendant stands up straight in front of the court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' reads as 'in front of' in the surface, and also gives ERE; it does both jobs honestly.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe a body or post held upright rather than leaning.

clue.text: Jack put on feminine Parisian article for some time

indicators.note: in a down entry, what is put on something sits on top of it

explanation.surface: A man called Jack puts on a woman's French garment for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on' in a down clue sets J above UNE. 'Article' looks like clothing; it is a grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a month is a stretch of time, and 'some' flags that this is only one instance.

clue.text: Specify page should wear tailored teal suit

indicators.note: a tailored suit is cut and shaped, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A pageboy is told to wear a made-to-measure blue-green suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Page' is a boy in a wedding party in the surface; in the wordplay it is just P.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to state a requirement exactly, as in a contract.

clue.text: Partner-swapping in the dark is something to behold

indicators.note: in bridge North and South are partners, so swapping partners changes one for the other

explanation.surface: Racy goings-on in darkness make quite a spectacle.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge partners are North and South; swapping N for S in NIGHT gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sight is a spectacle, a thing worth seeing or beholding.

clue.text: Go before end of game, give up on promotion

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

parts.note: to cede is to give up or surrender

explanation.surface: A player quits before the game ends, abandoning hope of going up a division.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Promotion' looks like a team going up a league, which suits the game; it means publicity. In an across clue, 'on' puts the first pieces after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to come earlier in time or order, as the Latin 'cedere', to go, suggests.

clue.text: American vessel in Tilbury to empty somewhere in Italy

indicators.note: in places the American and vessel inside what is left of Tilbury
emptying Tilbury removes its inside, leaving just the first and last letters

parts.note: a can is a container or vessel

explanation.surface: An American ship docks at Tilbury, an English port, ready to unload for Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuscany is a region of central Italy, so it is a place within that country.
